I bought this because everyone said it was a fun co-op survival game.

Five hours later I'm starving, freezing, insane, and learning that a winter hat somehow requires more resources than building a house.

Fine. I'll join a public server instead.

There are 200 servers, 180 of them are in Chinese, half have 60 mods installed, everyone is on day 4000, and they're speaking in abbreviations I've never seen before while I'm still trying to figure out why my berries keep rotting.

Winter arrives.

Our campfire is barely alive. One friend is hallucinating shadow creatures, another is freezing to death, our food is gone, and then Deerclops decides it's his turn. The fire goes out. Everyone dies in the dumbest way imaginable. We spend the next hour trying to recover our backpacks only to die again.

People will tell you the game gets easier.

It doesn't.

It just changes from "How do I survive tonight?" to "How do I spend the next 600 days collecting twigs, grass, manure, and berries again?" Every boss is solved by watching the same 25-minute YouTube guide with a thumbnail full of red arrows and circles, every public lobby somehow has one guy telling everyone they're playing wrong, and somehow the community has turned "survived 10,000 days" into a personality trait.

If you're thinking about buying this game, don't.

Save yourself while you still can.

Or don't. We'll see you starving around the campfire in a few days anyway.

In all seriousness, here's my actual review, since I feel that it deserves one.
This game has an [i]insane[/i] amount of replayability, combined with a near infinite amount of ways to play it. One person could be a complete and utter warlord trying to defeat all the bosses the game has to offer, while another could just be trying to recruit all the pigs they see and give them unique hats; extraordinarily, both of these playstyles can coexist with each other in this game. 
The first few hours of the game are infuriating. You die so many times that you might give up on playing it entirely. Then you come back and look at guides to get good. Then you keep dying until you stop dying, and now you suddenly have a hundred hours into the game; even with that, you're still finding out new ways to play the game and get better at not dying. You still somehow die anyways, because this game's few core mechanics are so well-done that ignoring one of them may or may not come back to bite you in the rear.
The only thing that really separates the newbies and the veterans in this game is the amount of knowledge they have in the game, and yet the game has so many ways to be played and further optimized that there really isn't a definitive way to even say who's the most professional at not starving and who isn't.

All things considered, saying that the game is "pretty good" might be an understatement. It's so good that it probably made me forget to not starve in real life at one point.
Personally, I may have played this game too much. But one of my personal favorite things about this game is that even though the sandbox part of the game is encouraged at some points, it isn't crucial to the experience; it's made my own goal of being an all-conquering war god very enjoyable. The fighting is quite simplistic, but with how the enemies and bosses of the game are designed, it's probably for the best that fighting is simple; one trip-up can cost you your entire game, and the way the bosses challenge your knowledge of the game makes for battles that have made me have a heart attack a few times -- looking at you, Misery Toadstool.

In addition to all of that, there's a cherry on top of the cherry, too; the developers of this game are great. They respect the community, and use their criticisms to make the game better -- they even let the spiders wear hats!

So, yeah. Good game. Good devs too. Still utterly despise those demonic monkeys in the Ruins, though.

[h1] Don’t Starve Together: A Thrilling Survival Experience [/h1]

[h1] Overview [/h1]
Don’t Starve Together is a multiplayer survival game by Klei Entertainment, building on the success of the original Don’t Starve. Players are thrown into a dark, eerie world filled with challenges and must cooperate (or compete) to survive. The game features a unique art style, intriguing lore, and demanding gameplay mechanics that test creativity and strategy.

[h1] Story and Atmosphere [/h1]
The game’s lore is subtle yet engaging. Players are stranded in the Constant, a mysterious world filled with strange creatures and environmental hazards. The story unfolds through exploration and scattered clues, leaving much to player interpretation. The gothic hand-drawn art style and atmospheric music amplify the eerie, survival-focused tone.

[h1] Gameplay [/h1]
At its core, the game is about survival—gathering resources, crafting items, and fending off dangers such as hunger, darkness, and hostile creatures. Multiplayer introduces new dynamics, requiring teamwork to split tasks, defend against threats, and manage limited resources. The challenge increases with changing seasons, each bringing unique obstacles like freezing winters or scorching summers.

[h1] Pros[/h1]
[list]
    [*]Unique Art Style: The hand-drawn, Tim Burton-esque visuals stand out.
    [*]Replayability: Randomized worlds and dynamic challenges keep the experience fresh.
    [*]Multiplayer Depth: Cooperative gameplay adds layers of strategy and fun.
    [*]Challenging Yet Rewarding: Success feels earned due to the game’s difficulty.
[/list]

[h1] Cons [/h1]
[list]
    [*]Steep Learning Curve: The lack of hand-holding can overwhelm newcomers.
    [*]Resource Management Pressure: Balancing food, sanity, and health can feel repetitive.
    [*]Team Dependency: Multiplayer can frustrate if teammates are inexperienced or uncooperative.
[/list]

[h1] Final [/h1]
Don’t Starve Together is a creative and challenging survival experience that rewards teamwork and strategy. While it may not suit players seeking a casual experience, fans of survival games will appreciate its depth and charm.

The goal of Don't Starve Together is to find and fight all ~ 26 boss monsters, a lot of which can be more or less hidden.

Two of these bosses are considered "final bosses" in the sense that killing them is the big accomplishment of two separate journeys with many different steps, one taking you deep in horribly dangerous underground dungeons and one taking you all around the sea.
After each of these 2 bosses, new content is added in the form of new "post game" world modifications that each gives new bosses, new mechanics, new weapons, armor and technologies to use.

I wanted to start by describing that because DST looks deceptively more simple than it truly is when you first take a look a it, when in truth it actually is quite complex, rich and intricate!



In this game, surviving is tough and difficult and requires you to understand a lot of different specific steps, and understand how many resources are tied together or meant to be exploited in strange and unexpected ways.
At first it feels like learning to stay alive during each of the 4 seasons is the game, and it won't necessarily make you feel like it's super deep because it is actually only step one. It's supposed to be simple and slow! It's possible to survive a year without too much trouble in a kind of baren base with not so much stuff at your disposal, but that is very far from the goal, which is about learning to thrive and accumulate wealth in order to get out there and fight bosses (that won't come to you unless you come to them.)

There are lots of different resources you can take from the world and bring back home, creatures who'se homes you can move, beneficial structures you can acquire, all kinds of things that are meant to saturate you in food, tools, weapons and armors for your many expeditions.

But the game never holds your hand through any of it at all. Learning can be really unclear and counter-intuitive (who would think that butterflies are the most basic and most essential source of food early game, or that you are supposed to relocate pig houses around a pen in order to have a steady supply of armor every full moon? No one, at first!) and every step of the way can make you think "is that it?" just because you may likely fail to see the link between things for a while, or how you are meant to abuse the heck out of them, or how they are just stepping stones towards something bigger.
It's a game that you just won't be able to enjoy if you struggle with challenging yourself. You need to throw yourself out there, be active, be looking to learn and practice survival techniques and get busy trying to do things on a grander scale, or do research about which bosses should be next and how to reach them.
Knowledge is either difficult to acquire on your own or requires you to practice several times to get it right, and then so much better than right. It can be intimidating, which can make you become a bit too passive and invite boredom because you're nowhere near having completed all there is to complete, but you may not understand how to get there, or how to learn.

Nothing research and interacting with the community can't fix though!
I regularily give many tips and explanations to people from a particular discord community server, it's a great vibe.



All in all, I recommend this game with all of my heart with the knowledge that it really may not be for everybody, especially if you tend to be too passive or can't bother with putting too much effort into trying to overcome challenges. 
It's my own favorite survival game out there specifically because it gives survival so much purpose and so many steps, because of how much effort you can put into learning and how rewarding it can be; but it can put some people off.

There's a lot of ways to achieve the same things. Tons of different knowledge, a bunch of different mechanics that you will likely gloss over for a couple hundred hours until you start using them and start realizing "why have I never bothered doing this awesome thing before" (like taming and riding big cows to become the ultimate war machine) 
There's fun in joining random worlds and seeing how you can contribute, fun in starting over and doing things better and quicker or in different order, fun in practicing the same skills because they're tough and require good habits, fun in seeing how everyone's lack of knowledge can create so many shenanigans due to lack of preparation, lack of resources, lack of having made enough structures in time, and fun in modding the game and tweaking the little things along the way.

There's lots to love!

[h3] Okay guys, I played a little bit... It's time to finally write a review. I promise to be concise. [/h3]
This game is annoyingly obstinate in theme, design, and user interface. It comes packaged with a flimsy combat system, deliberately useless-sounding/actually-useless tools & structures, and a slightly uncanny and weird art style that's honestly something you just have to see for yourself.

[h3] This game is also kind of... hard. Maybe in a bad way. [/h3]
Seriously? Well, this is a positive review. I'll explain. Nothing gets explained to the player, and players basically just have to point and click on random stuff, make some random tools, and either die of darkness, or die of boredom once they've been sitting at a campfire for 8 minutes straight. If they survive longer, then they die of hounds. Live a little longer? Die to insanity. If somehow they make it to Winter... well, you can guess. I don't have any large praise for this game design, as while I look at this learning process fondly now... it's really frustrating at its core to be entirely honest. I was definitely interested in the game a LOT, don't get me wrong. There's no way I could have possibly played as much as I have now and probably more in the future if I didn't enjoy this, but this game is deliberately difficult: accomplished through ignorance and severely punishing mistakes. Y'know, as a solo-player game, I'd leave it at that, but there's more.

[h3] This game was not meant to be played alone. To that end, it is a lot like another game we all know and love. [/h3]
Minecraft. I think it's a lot like Don't Starve -- maybe not in genre -- but in the sense that the way players learn how to play the game is shockingly a bit similar. In Minecraft, not a whole lot is really explained, and I feel like, to a stranger, you can only really explain it as a game where you play with lego blocks and make crappy log cabins... like, forever (sounds boring?). 

Anyways, No One Learned How To Play Minecraft On Their Own. Seriously, how did anyone learn how to build their first nether portal? How did anyone figure out the ending of the game and all of the steps that led up to defeating the ender dragon? We all learned it through each other. Older siblings, friends, school peers, those crappy Minecraft journals at the book faire, ONLINE guides? That's how we learned, and that's how the public understanding of Minecraft became so advanced, for an otherwise obtuse and poorly explained game. 

[h3] That's Don't Starve. [/h3]
Dropping in on public servers, toiling away like a dolt, barely surviving with a few other, dull campers until some Enlightened Soul steps in to your base to actually organize it and show you the ropes of the game. You'd learn about crockpots, iceboxes, you might really get into base-building. Later, you'd learn about all the biomes, find out how to survive the seasons, start exploring the caves, etc. All at the advice of others in public lobbies or on the internet. All of the pitfalls of Don't Starve's deliberately difficult design and the obscure knowledge that players have to learn are all elements that make mentors and collaboration even more valuable. We all taught each other, and while this game did not truly start out as a multiplayer game... 

[b] I think I can at least say that the experience of sharing knowledge, learning the ropes, and tutoring new, acolyte survivors in this stupid, obtuse little survival game was truly valuable in the end. Don't Starve guys. [/b]

It's a Victorian Style survival game with co-op, the game can be quite hard, but if you make your own world you can adjust it to be easier If you so desire. The game receives decent updates and as of now most characters I believe have had reworks done to them.

This game is really about teamwork.
You have to share food, supplies, weapons, and clothes between all players to survive longer (which is the goal of this game). The game saves your progress automatically with each new day so you can continue playing in the same world. You don't have to play until you're starving in game and/or in the real world :D

Don't Starve Together is a game that I can say quite a lot about even as someone who hasn't played the original Don't Starve. If you are wanting to buy this game, but you intend to only play it by yourself, then I strongly suggest you stop now, don't get this game, and get the original Don't Starve along with its DLCs instead. If you still want to get this game, then I'm just going to say that there is a lot to learn about this game and you'll need to know stuff about the original Don't Starve as well. 

You don't need to know the plot of the original game to know what Don't Starve is about. Even though it is a sequel in a way, you don't need to know what happened. Basically, you're going to be dropped into a world and you are going to have only one goal, survive as long as you can. There is a lore to the game, and it is an incredibly rich lore that should definitely get some sort of attention because it's really interesting and ever so more expanding. The world is already interesting enough with the kind of creatures it holds and what each of the playable characters can do, but it's that lore that does make this world all the much the better once you know it. 

Right off the bat, the game spews charm from it. From character and monster designs, to the artstyle, the old vintage look, and even down the music which sounds like what you would imagine the world would have. I can sit on the main menu of this game for hours to listen to the theme. 

You'll have 12 characters to pick and choose who you'll play as, each one with different stats and different abilities that make them stand out from each other. For players who have already played Don't Starve, you won't have to worry about these characters needing to be unlocked, they're all unlocked right out of the gate. Also for players who have played Don't Starve, the characters have changed a bit in order to be a bit more balanced for multiplayer. Each character fits a different play style so you'll never feel as though you're playing as the same character, and you can feel the differences with each character and you'll find someone with a playstyle who you'll enjoy playing as the most.

This game is not easy and if you are new, you'll probably not survive for very long in it especially if you do not know what to do. The game is not going to teach you anything, you'll either have to learn to survive as you play, learn from other players, or research about the game. At no point are you ever going to be safe. You'll have to eat to keep yourself from starving, find ways to restore your character's sanity so that way you don't go insane and be attacked by shadow creatures, fire can spread and destroy precious resources, some resources can't respawn, some creatures will attack and try to kill you, and there will be a pack of hounds that will randomly come after you as you go through each day. Even changing seasons will be a hazard as you'll either have to survive the cold of winter, the storms of spring, or the heat of summer. It may be hard to get into first, but once you get a grasp of the game and how it plays, it feels so satisifying to be able to survive longer than you used to. You'll need to craft items to survive and even craft items to craft even more items and you'll need as much as you can and know exactly what you need to survive for so long.

The one thing that stands about this game over the original Don't Starve is that this one has online multiplayer where you can play up to 6 other people. You can play by yourself, but it won't be easier than playing with others unless you have mods supported by the Steam Workshop. If you're going to play this game with others, I highly recommend playing with friends. 

If there is one thing I can say about this game is that it will get reptitive. Once you get the hang of the game, it's just a matter of surviving as long as you can and if you are able to learn the game to the point where you know everything about it, you'll have nearly nothing to worry about. 

If you want a challenging survival game and one that you can play with friends, this game is definitely for you and I can highly recommend it to others. Even though it can get repetitive after a while, I still find it to be a fun game where you'll always have to be doing something to survive and keep going, and with the developers continuing to add more stuff to the game and showing a great passion for it, I can see it being supported for a long time.

Introduction:
Don't Starve Together, developed by Klei Entertainment, is an exceptional multiplayer survival game that expands upon the dark and whimsical world of its predecessor, Don't Starve. This standalone multiplayer version allows players to brave the unforgiving wilderness together, fostering cooperation and strategic planning as they strive to survive in a beautifully atmospheric and challenging environment. With its unique art style, compelling gameplay mechanics, and richly immersive world, Don't Starve Together delivers an unforgettable co-op survival experience.

Gameplay:
At its core, Don't Starve Together revolves around the struggle for survival in a harsh and unpredictable wilderness. Players must gather resources, craft tools and structures, explore dangerous biomes, and, of course, manage their hunger, sanity, and health. The game emphasizes collaboration and communication, as players can work together to tackle complex challenges and share the responsibilities of survival.

The game features a plethora of intriguing characters, each with their own unique abilities and playstyles. From the scientific-minded Wilson to the mighty Wolfgang or the enigmatic Maxwell, every character adds depth and variety to the gameplay. Selecting the right combination of characters within your group is essential for tackling the game's diverse challenges effectively.

Exploration is a key aspect of Don't Starve Together, as the world is procedurally generated and filled with mysteries, hidden treasures, and dangerous creatures. Each playthrough presents new discoveries and surprises, encouraging players to continually explore and adapt their strategies. The dynamic day and night cycle, seasonal changes, and the looming threat of darkness and supernatural forces create an ever-present sense of tension and urgency.

In addition to survival aspects, the game incorporates a robust crafting system, allowing players to create a wide range of tools, weapons, structures, and even magical items. Experimentation and resource management play significant roles, as players must gather specific materials and combine them strategically to survive and thrive. The depth of the crafting system provides ample opportunities for creativity and strategic decision-making.

Features:

    Cooperative Multiplayer: Don't Starve Together shines brightest in its multiplayer mode, where players can team up with friends or other online adventurers. Working together, sharing resources, and coordinating tasks amplify the game's survival elements, fostering a sense of camaraderie and shared accomplishment.

    Engaging Characters: The diverse cast of playable characters in Don't Starve Together offers distinct abilities, strengths, and weaknesses. Experimenting with different character combinations adds depth to the gameplay, as players can devise unique strategies and capitalize on each character's skills.

    Unforgiving Challenge: Don't Starve Together's difficulty level strikes a fine balance, providing an enjoyable challenge without being excessively punishing. Survival requires careful planning, adaptation to changing conditions, and efficient resource management. This blend of challenge and reward keeps players engaged and invested in the game's world.

    Unique Art Style and Atmosphere: The hand-drawn art style of Don't Starve Together is visually stunning and distinctive. With its macabre yet whimsical aesthetic, the game's visuals evoke a sense of eerie beauty. Coupled with haunting ambient sounds and a hauntingly enchanting musical score, the atmosphere immerses players in a world teeming with mystery and danger.

    Regular Updates and Community Support: Klei Entertainment has shown a commendable dedication to supporting and expanding the game since its launch. The developers regularly release content updates, bug fixes, and balance adjustments, ensuring that the game remains fresh and enjoyable. The active and passionate community further enhances the experience, providing mods, guides, and multiplayer servers that extend the game's longevity.

With its engaging gameplay, cooperative mechanics, atmospheric visuals, and constant sense of discovery, the game captivates players and keeps them hooked for hours on end. Klei Entertainment's commitment to ongoing support and community engagement ensures that Don't Starve Together remains a vibrant and evolving multiplayer survival adventure. Various beasts, catastrophes, shadow figures or feeble-minded pigs might cross your way and won't make it easy for you to stay alive in this rough world. So why not invite some friends? The title says it all, other than the Singleplayer: "Don't Starve" here you should probably bring some company to explore the world and exist against those horrible creatures. But if it wasn't difficult enough.. the weather won't be on your side for long either. It might be rather challenging to play this Game and there are a lot of mechanics and tricks that make DST unique, but you will need quite some experience to figure them out.
The very charming graphics and humor will make you love the Game quicker than you want.[/i]
 
[u]Characters:[/u]
You can select from a lot of different characters for your journey, who all have their very personal Pros & Cons.
The specific abilities and weaknesses make the gameplay exciting and miscellaneous everytime again, trust me..
From Robots and Spiders to Scientists and Warrior Valkyries your choice is kind of unlimited (even more and better characters are still developed) and up to you and your fellow survivors.

[u]Base Building:[/u]
Of course you can wander around as a Nomad, gather ressources and be on track all the time but the essence to be progressive in DST is to build yourself a base for all your needs, I mean who wouldn't prefer some delicious Meatballs fresh from the crockpot over berries and carrots..
In order to set up your buildings you can't just immediately cobble together some boards and stones like a pig.. You have to invent them before! By the huge variety of items in the Game it won't be easy to obtain them all. So good luck.

[u]Boss Creatures:[/u]
Every now and then some more or less scary Meanies will come to destroy your well deserved progress! Better be prepared and packed with armor, weapons and perhaps some magical items to defeat them. *Psst* They also have unique loot which will grant you access to craft cool gadgets or equipments to make your living easier :)

[u]The Caves:[/u]
On the one hand there's the actually quite harmless overworld with its rich land but on the other there's also the underground which has a lot of dangerous and scary beasts lurking for you in the darkness! But if you can prevail down there, you will probably be abled to find the magical secrets of the ruins, which should be discovered by yourself. Once you have beaten them you can rule the overworld with your knowledge!

[h1]Skins (and how to get them)[/h1]
Yes, here you'll also find those Skins for Items you might already know from other Games ^^
Don't worry.. they're just cosmetic and won't give you any advantage! Besides the advantage of spicy looking characters, tools or buildings. And you can even share the skins on tools or buildings with your friends in-game, so everyone profits from them ;)

You get 1 Skin Drop everyday by logging in and 8 Skin Drops every week by playing (Caution! Science required)
Some might be marketable and some might not be, but they look cool non the less :D
You can also purchase Skin Collections in the Shop of the Game to support the Developers!
And maybe you're lucky and you can even make some money of selling or trading them :}


[b]The Game is definitely worth the full-price and the long time motivation is assured![/b]

After 1,000+ hours I realized something. 

Don't Starve Together is NOT a game. I repeat, NOT a game.

It is instead a beautifully crafted "LANGUAGE" that you wrestle with, learn, and eventually try to share it with friends. 

Starting off in either Don't Starve or in DST, you'll have quite the traditional uncompromising experience.
Like learning any new language it does not make any sense right off the bat.

One important thing that a good coach taught me when learning a secondary language is:
"It's gonna hurt. A lot. It won't be easy." 

But understanding that fact alone actually makes it easier. It braces you. 

You keep speaking it, converse with others, slip up a bit, and eventually you get a bit of a grasp. 

And even if you think you understand it. You're not done.

DST has come along nicely over the years with continued updates and support by Klei.
Quality of life additions such as being able to search for crafts in game, and integrating a local geometric placement option to name a few things are nice touches. That on top of added character skills and adjusted recipes, I would say DST is more chewable now for the new or returning players who are interested.

Some of Klei's games can be swing or miss for me, but this has remained a shining home run through and through. 

If there's anything you get from this review it should be to just get it. Especially if it's on sale.

If you want to experience a product that is actually made with love, in addition to being something that rewards a players curiosity and creativity in all the right ways, this is it! 

Learning how to get through your first Winter, discovering a new hatred for frogs, and fighting over the last meat ball in the Ice Box in a pub of 5 people will go from being frustrating moments, to memorable wholesome experiences on your journey through the Constant. 

Then, when you hit your first 100 days in a solo world you'll say to yourself: "Thank God there are no mimes here..." 

Each day you spend in Don't Starve will be about refinement. Looking up new info, recipes, figuring out how to fight off your first few hound waves, seeing your friend die to a lightning strike one Spring, and with a bit of patience it opens up more and more.

You'll find that one character that just feels right, and who will probably get better with updates.

You'll kill that stupid bear, goose, thing for the first time and wear its pelt. 

You'll learn that there's a world option to turn off Summer completely, and get very tempted to do so...

But most importantly, hopefully, you'll learn that this a true gem to learn alongside friends. A language can't be fully learned alone. 

It's satisfying to finally comb those caves on your own. But, with a pal or two it can just be a whole new experience.

I even encourage checking out people hosting publics or join a Klei-hosted server. Some of the best community around is right here. Play and meet people. Ask questions. Die to a tentacle. Enjoy the process. 

I don't think I will ever learn how to fully speak French, but I can tell you that DST is a full and wonderful experience. Get it if you can, get it for a friend.

And remember, always stay near the light. It's hard to study in the dark.

This is a fun co-op survival game, though game mechanics discourage larger servers. 

Dead players bring the 'sanity' of live players down, so on large servers (which are more likely to have a dead player at any given moment), your 'sanity' is threatened more often. Resurrecting dead players becomes a larger part of the game on these servers. 

Communication is much more important on large servers. With more players, the chance of running into a serious threat increases. Dealing with those threats sometimes requires a quick response and that is much harder to accomplish when there is no easy way to tell where teammates are short of clear and frequent communication.

On top of those challenges, having many players occupy the same bit of land leads to a greater chance of resource scarcity. On small servers, this isn't as much of an issue. On large servers, often vital resources have been picked dry when a new player joins the server, leaving them to face the night with no fire or weapon.

All of these problems can be addressed by the players with some forethought and planning, but these are issues unique to larger servers. If you play alone or with 1-2 other people, then the game is challenging without having to worry about these additional challenges. Of course, if you want a significantly greater challenge than what the single player or small server game offers, then a large server is for you. Aside from the disparity in difficulty between small and large servers, this game is everything you could want from a multiplayer experience of 'Don't Starve.' Everything that made the single player game great is here. If you ever get frustrated with the large server experience, then you can always dial it back down to a more manageable challenge.

The difficulty is that those who have played a lot of dont starve have so much more expertese than those who have never played it that it's the equivalent of a wilderness survival guide taking an 8 year old city kid camping.

There are PVP servers, avoid them if you arent experienced in the game, it's not the way most of us play it, but some people love it that way.  New players joining these servers are fodder.  Joining an open Co-op world you may be able to find someone to help you.
